by dead reckoning near Cape Adelaide, James Ross's magnetic pole of 1831

cook-1908-axel-heiberg-002.title: Back to land: Hassel Sound to Cape Sparbo, June-September 1908

Penny Strait between Bathurst Island and Grinnell Peninsula; makes for the Devon shore (date inferred)
begins the climb over the highlands of Grinnell Peninsula in rain, then two days storm-bound
descends to Eidsbotn; no game; the last dogs are set free and the party takes to the canvas boat
driven on a berg past Hell Gate and Cardigan Strait, losing a fortnight in a day (date inferred)
lands at Cape Vera on Devon Island; a hare taken (date inferred)
passes Belcher Point at midnight as the sun sets for the first time
eastward ten miles, then beset in a nameless glacier bay; new ice forms around the boat

reaches Cape Sparbo with a half sledge, a torn tent and four cartridges

north along the Ellesmere coast; a short pass taken through Talbot Inlet (date inferred)

Cape Sabine; Panikpah's year-old seal cache found, marked with a drawing of his search for his son (date inferred)
crosses Smith Sound and reaches Annoatok; met by Harry Whitney (date inferred, mid-April)

crocker-land-1913-078.title: The voyage north: Brooklyn to Etah in the Diana and the Erik, July-August 1913

waypoints.note: the Diana of St John's, chartered by the American Museum, loading at the Brooklyn Navy-yard: 10,000 lb of biscuit, 5,000 of flour, 10,000 gallons of kerosene. The book gives no date for leaving New York
Boston: 14,000 lb of pemmican taken in; 'friends and relatives steamed down the harbor with us on the afternoon of the 5th'
Sydney, Cape Breton: 30,000 lb of English dog-biscuit and 13,000 feet of matched spruce for the house at Etah
North Sydney: sails at five in the afternoon, 'our long two-thousand-mile trip had begun'
Red Bay, Labrador: 'the lights in the fishermen's huts of Red Bay winked and blinked us to sleep'

Barge Point: a little after midnight the Diana strikes, 'as if the very bottom was being ripped completely out of her'. The Newfoundland government steamer Stella Maris comes round the point on the 17th
Battle Harbour: the hull examined and the Diana condemned for the ice
St John's: the sealer Erik taken over from Job Brothers in the Diana's place
back at Battle Harbour; the stores left there reloaded into the Erik
'on the 5th we were again headed toward the North'. A gale in Baffin Bay on the 6th, 7th and 8th
the Arctic Circle crossed
Melville Bay in thick fog, the 'Bergy Hole'; at 10 p.m. the fog lifts on the basalt shaft of the Devil's Thumb
at 12.30 p.m. the whistle blown under the cliffs of Cape York; the Inughuit come out in kayaks
Umanak (North Star Bay) at 2 a.m.; Panikpa and his sons Ka-ko-tchee-a and E-took-a-shoo come aboard. A polar bear shot off Cape Parry
Ig-loo-da-houny in Murchison Sound, where a large camp of Inughuit is found; Arklio, Teddy-ling-wa and Tau-ching-wa taken on, and at Nerky Noo-ka-ping-wa and Oo-bloo-ya
Etah at 11 p.m.; Ah-pellah taken on for his knowledge of the country to the west
after a week of failed attempts to cross Smith Sound to Flagler Bay, the ship is moored to the rocks of Provision Point and the stores are landed at Etah instead
the Erik blows her whistle, dips her flag and is out of sight round Cape Alexander. The expedition is on its own for what it expects to be two years

crocker-land-1913-079.title: The first relief: the George B. Cluett, 1915-1916

waypoints.note: the three-masted auxiliary schooner George B. Cluett, Captain Charles Pickles, chartered by the American Museum, reaches Umanak (North Star Bay) with a disabled engine after crossing ice-choked Melville Bay with no one aboard who knew that water. Hovey and Comer decide she shall stay in that port

Hovey goes on the last hundred miles to Etah in the Danish station's power-boat, with Freuchen's help, and finds MacMillan and Small at Etah. He offers to take them home; MacMillan chooses to stay another year
the Cluett is caught and frozen in for the winter at Parker Snow Bay
MacMillan sledges down from Etah and reaches the beset ship
the Cluett breaks out of the ice; Captain Pickles refuses to take her further north
she sails for home with Hovey and Hunt aboard, leaving four of the men she had come for still in the North
the Danmark is chartered from Copenhagen by the American Museum to go to Etah from South Greenland and bring the expedition and its collections to Sydney, Cape Breton. The book gives no sailing date

she reaches Umanak (North Star Bay) on 23 September, a month too late for Smith Sound, and goes into winter quarters. She is provisioned for thirty men to 1 November 1917; MacMillan's party will not leave Borup Lodge for her
Ekblaw and Hunt leave the beset ship to sledge south across Melville Bay, judging that she will never reach Etah and that under sail alone the passage home would be long
she cannot get out of the ice before August 1917, and with little coal might have trouble even then

crocker-land-1913-081.title: The ship that came: the SS Neptune, Etah to Sydney, August 1917

waypoints.note: the SS Neptune, Captain Robert Bartlett, comes into Foulke Fiord with her siren going, painted battleship gray and her mainmast gone. 'Is that you, Bob?'
the expedition, its collections and its dogs are taken aboard and Etah is left after four years
at Clarence Head, on the Ellesmere side, a solid mass of ice and not a lead to be seen
the Cary Islands: locked in the ice for three days, two iron plates torn off the bows, all steam-pumps working and a plank well built in the forehold

Hakluyt Island, which Baffin named 300 years before and which was struck off the map with all of Baffin Bay until it was rediscovered: MacMillan, Bartlett and Burbank land and find old stone houses, tupik rings, storehouses and fox traps
Oo-loo-set on the western end of Northumberland Island; the Inughuit work their kayaks out through the moving drift ice to the ship
south to Cape Parry, where open water lets the ship get within twenty-five miles of Cape York; a call at the deserted village of Akbat

Bartlett steers boldly south into the pack, makes little, and retreats to the lee of Cape York. Sixty years before almost to the day the Fox had been locked in Melville Bay for 252 days and drifted 1,194 miles
at noon the Neptune swings on her heel for another try; at five she is in open water and going rapidly south
Godhavn (Qeqertarsuaq) on Disko: the old whaler's lookout, the hulk of the Fox, and Ekblaw, who had sledged out of Melville Bay the winter before. The trip south begins at 1.30 on the 17th

a dark line on the starboard bow on the morning of the 22nd: Labrador, the first sight of the Southland. A few hours at Turnavik, the Bartlett fishing-station, and despatches sent by wireless from the Makkovik station
Sydney Harbour on the morning of the 24th: boarded and inspected, and let through the line of chained pontoons - the expedition's first touch of the war that had begun while it was away

davis-baffin-hudson-001.title: Davis's first voyage: the Sunneshine and the Moonshine, 1585

waypoints.note: leaves Dartmouth with the Sunneshine (50 tons) and the Moonshine (35 tons)
held at Falmouth by contrary winds until 13 June
held in the Scilly Isles until 28 June, sounding and surveying the roads

south along the shore to double Cape Farewell, driftwood and seals about the ship

leaves Gilbert Sound and stands north-west across the strait that now carries Davis's name
the Baffin coast: Mount Raleigh, Totnes Road, Exeter Sound, Dyer's Cape and Cape Walsingham named in one day
Cape of God's Mercy, the north point of the entrance to Cumberland Sound
sixty leagues north-west into Cumberland Sound; the ships part company round islands in the middle of it for five days
ashore: a stone wall, a human skull, twenty collared dogs, two sledges, one of fir boards and one of whalebone
turns back down the sound, the wind against them
loses sight of the north land of the entrance and steers for England
raises the Land of Desolation again; a storm that night separates the ships
England sighted
into Dartmouth

davis-baffin-hudson-002.title: Davis's second voyage: the Mermayde, Sunneshine, Moonelight and Northstarre, 1586

waypoints.note: leaves Dartmouth with four sail: Mermayde 120 tons, Sunneshine 60, Moonelight 35, and the ten-ton pinnace Northstarre
land at 60 deg, 47 deg west of London, ice lying up to fifty leagues off; forced south to 57 deg to double it
anchors again within the isles of Gilbert Sound; the people remember the English of the year before
forty Kalaallit help launch the pinnace; leaping and wrestling matches, and a fire kindled by drill that Davis takes for sorcery
a man seized as a hostage for a stolen anchor, then carried to sea when the wind came fair. The margin of the printed text reads that he afterwards died
at 63 deg 8 min, a mighty and strange quantity of ice in one entire mass
trading for skins near Old Sukkertoppen; the speech here is plainer, not hollow in the throat
Davis goes on in the Moonelight, leaving the Mermayde at anchor to sail for England
fifty leagues west, land in 66 deg 19 min: the Baffin coast about Cape Walsingham

anchors in a fair road; from a hilltop Davis sees the land is all islands. Markham puts him on Resolution Island, at the mouth of Hudson Strait, without knowing it
a fair harbour in 56 deg on the Labrador coast, sailed ten leagues in, fir, pine, alder, yew and birch on both sides
in 54 deg 30 min, cod taken as fast as the hook goes over
anchors among low wooded isles; eight leagues north a mighty great sea passing between two lands west, probably Hamilton Inlet
five young sailors ashore for fish are attacked from the wood: two killed by arrows, two badly wounded, one escapes by swimming
after five days of storm, departs for England
the Sunneshine into Dartmouth; Davis writes to Sanderson from Exeter on 14 October

davis-baffin-hudson-003.title: Davis's third voyage: the Elizabeth, Sunneshine and the pinnace Ellen, 1587

waypoints.note: leaves Dartmouth at midnight with the Elizabeth, the Sunneshine and a clinker-built pinnace, the Ellen, of perhaps twenty tons
land sighted on the west Greenland coast between Paamiut and Qeqertarsuatsiaat; Cape Farewell rounded without being seen
anchors among low islands in 64 deg: Gilbert Sound again, the people crying Iliaout and showing sealskins
the master of the Sunneshine seizes a strong lusty young man and carries him aboard; what became of him is not related
at two in the morning the upper strakes are torn off the new pinnace for the iron in them; the gunner fires a saker with no ball in it and everyone runs
Davis goes north in the Ellen; the Elizabeth and Sunneshine are to fish on the west side between 54 and 55 deg and wait for him
in 67 deg 40 min, whales and easy trading along the shore
72 deg 12 min at noon and at midnight, variation 28 deg west: the farthest north, named Hope Sanderson for William Sanderson. The sea open to the west and north
stands west and runs forty leagues and better without sight of land
falls in with a mighty bank of ice lying north and south, the middle pack of Baffin Bay, and is forced to coast it southward
Mount Raleigh on the Baffin coast again
anchors in Cumberland Sound and names the Earl of Cumberland's Isles
Bruton and some of the mariners ashore find many graves and train oil spilt on the ground, the dogs so fat they were scant able to run
clear out of the sound, at noon in 64 deg of latitude
passes a great inlet between 63 and 62 deg, named Lumley's Inlet: the water whirling and overfalling as if it were the fall of some great water through a bridge

Warwick's Foreland; the bark falls into one of the overfalls under full sail and an ice island passes it going the other way. That day and night, a very great gulf, the water whirling and roaring as it were the meeting of tides
the southernmost cape of the gulf, named Chidley's Cape, put by Davis in 60 deg 10 min
Darcy's Island; deer swim away from the boat. Davis works south to the appointed fishing station and finds both ships gone home
lands in England all weary, having come home in the pinnace; writes to Sanderson from Sandridge the next day

Akpatok Island ('Desire Provoketh')

davis-baffin-hudson-005.title: Sir Thomas Button in the Resolution and the Discovery, 1612-1613

waypoints.note: inferred: leaves London in the Resolution with the Discovery, Captain John Ingram; no exact day is recorded
inferred: anchors at the Digges Islands as instructed and assembles a pinnace; five men are killed here
inferred: falls in with the west shore of the bay in about 60 deg 40 min and names it Hopes Checked, the first European crossing of Hudson Bay
takes harbour in Port Nelson and names the river for his sailing master Nelson, whom he buried there; Pricket gives the 13th and Button's own board says the 27th
the river finally freezes over, after several thaws; Button had been sick all winter and began to mend on 24 January
the ice clears from the river; many men are dead and the Resolution has to be abandoned
back off Hopes Checked; from here the only account is Sir Thomas Roe's abstract of Button's lost journal
inferred: names Hopes Advance, somewhere on the north-west shore; the identification is uncertain
his farthest north, about 65 deg, in the strait later named Sir Thomas Roe's Welcome; marked Ne Ultra on the old charts

davis-baffin-hudson-006.title: Bylot and Baffin in the Discovery, 1615: Hudson Strait and Foxe Channel

waypoints.note: inferred: Discovery weighs anchor at St Katherine's, London, Robert Bylot master, William Baffin mate/pilot
inferred: passes Gravesend outward bound, 14 men and 2 boys besides Bylot and Baffin
sights Resolution Island, entrance to Hudson Strait (Baffin's lat 61°30'N)

complete lunar-distance observation for longitude worked near Broken Point; Baffin's computed longitude 74°05'W, lat 63°40'N (his first lunar taken at sea)

reaches Mill Island, named for the 'greate extremetye and grindinge of the ice' (Baffin's lat 64°00'N; lon inferred)

off Nottingham Island testing the tide a second time (Baffin's lat 62°45'N; lon inferred)
anchors off Digges Island, natives seen on the rocks, men kill 70 fowl (Baffin's lat 62°45'N; lon inferred)
passes Resolution Island homeward bound, out of sight
inferred: sights Cape Clear, Ireland
inferred: anchors in Plymouth Sound before dawn, no man lost

waypoints.note: inferred: Discovery sets sail from Gravesend, 17 persons, Bylot master, Baffin pilot
inferred: passes between Land's End and Scilly after weather delays at Dartmouth and Plymouth
first land seen off Greenland coast near Sukkertoppen; six people come fishing to the ship (Baffin's lat 65°20'N; lon inferred)
anchors near Davis's 'London Coast' (Disco Bay area); people flee in boats, leave dogs behind (Baffin's lat 70°20'N; lon inferred)
passes Hope Sanderson, John Davis's 1587 farthest point (lat 72°12'N per Davis; lon inferred)

inferred: anchors in and is driven from Wolstenholme Sound

farthest north of the voyage, off Hakluyt Island at the mouth of Sir Thomas Smith's Sound, which Baffin says 'runneth to the north of 78 degrees'; greatest compass variation he ever recorded, over five points (56 degrees)

inferred: reaches the entrance of Alderman Jones his Sound, boat sent ashore, sea morses seen

forced east through much ice off the Baffin Island coast, land seen at eight or nine leagues (Baffin's lat 68°N; lon inferred)
gives up seeking the west shore, in the indraft of the Cumberland Isles, cook Richard Waynam dies (Baffin's lat 65°40'N; lon inferred)
anchors in Cockin Sound, Greenland, for scurvy-grass to cure the sick (Baffin's lat 65°45'N, possibly a misprint for 65°25'; lon inferred)
inferred: anchors at Dover after a fast passage home

davis-baffin-hudson-008.title: Jens Munk's expedition: the Enhiorningen and the Lamprenen, 1619-1620

Munckenes (Resolution Island), north side of the entrance to Fretum Christian (Hudson Strait), in 61d20m

passes the Orkney Islands
arrives at Bergen, Norway

inferred: passes Mansell's Island

reaches an island off Cape Fullerton which he names Sir Thomas Roe's Welcome, then turns south down the west shore of the bay
inferred: in Churchill Bay, which he calls Hubart's Hope
inferred: enters Port Nelson to overhaul the ship; finds relics of Button's 1612-13 wintering, including an inscribed board
inferred: declares in his journal that all hope of a passage on this shore is at an end

reaches and names Cape Henrietta Maria (Wolstenholme's Ultimum Vale), joining his discoveries to Hudson's
inferred: lands on Mill Island

south down Peel Sound (inferred: the only route consistent with the besetment position)
Franklin Strait, past the west coast of Boothia (inferred)

franklin-search-020.title: Austin's squadron: Resolute, Assistance, Pioneer and Intrepid, 1850-51

off Upernavik, flying north in an open sea (Osborn pp. 36, 50)
Cape Shackleton; the ships tracked and towed north while Penny, taking another route, gains on them (Osborn pp. 43-49)
firmly beset in Melville Bay; between 20 and 31 July not seven miles were made good in the right direction (Osborn pp. 61-65)
Melville Bay mastered by steam, powder and men after forty days beset; the Felix and the Prince Albert caught up and taken in tow (Osborn pp. 69-70)
Cape York; the Inughuit come out over the ice, and the Pioneer steams along the Crimson Cliffs of Beverley (Osborn p. 72)
after two days lost to Adam Beck's story the squadron divides: Assistance and Intrepid to Wolstenholme Sound, the rest reeving through the pack into the West Water (Osborn pp. 72-73)
the Pioneer enters Pond's Bay; Osborn lands at Button Point, pulls down Inuit cairns before learning they mark blubber caches, and leaves a record and presents in the huts (Osborn pp. 74-75)
rejoins the Resolute off Possession Bay, where the North Star's record is found; course up Lancaster Sound (Osborn pp. 75-76)
off Croker Bay, between Cape Warrender and Cape Home (Osborn p. 77)

off Gascoigne Inlet the Sophia's boat, with Captain Stewart and Dr Sutherland, brings the news of Cape Riley and Beechey Island; the Pioneer runs aground rounding Beechey Island that night (Osborn pp. 81-86)
crossing Wellington Channel towards Barlow Inlet; communicates with De Haven (Osborn pp. 98-101)
at the floe edge between Cape Bunny and Griffith Island; De Haven hoists his colours and bears up for New York (Osborn pp. 106-107)
winter quarters: the four ships secured to the ice that extended unbroken from Griffith Island to Cape Martyr (Osborn pp. 107, 109). The date is Osborn's 'late September'
the ice shoots the squadron out into Barrow Strait 'by turning itself fairly round on a pivot' after eleven months (Osborn p. 181)

Assistance Harbour: Penny offers to take a steamer up Wellington Channel, Austin declines, Penny decides to go home; the steamers are detached for Jones Sound on the night of the 14th (Osborn pp. 182-184)
Jones Sound opens out in the Coburg Bay of the charts; Cape Leopold found to be an island (Osborn p. 184)
a boat trip to a great inlet near Whale Sound: turf, scurvy-grass and London-pride, 'and this in latitude 76 deg 52 min N.' The latitude is Osborn's, the longitude inferred (Osborn pp. 190-191)
'the farthest northern latitude reached by any of our squadron, viz., 77 degrees north latitude' (Osborn p. 194). The longitude is inferred
the Pioneer forces the pack and rejoins Resolute and Assistance off Cape Dudley Digges at 4 a.m. (Osborn p. 195)
the Intrepid found, the squadron reunited, and a memorandum issued that they were to go to Woolwich; homeward at eight o'clock (Osborn p. 206)
the latitude of Cape Farewell, eight days out (Osborn p. 207)
the Pioneer anchors at Grimsby in the Humber, three weeks from the start of the homeward voyage; the squadron paid off with the loss of one man out of 180 (Osborn p. 207)

franklin-search-024.title: Belcher in HMS Assistance with the Pioneer, 1852-1854

waypoints.note: the five-ship squadron leaves Greenhithe at 5 a.m. under Sir Edward Belcher (M'Dougall p. 3)
the Assistance reaches Beechey Island; Resolute and North Star are already secured to the floe there (Belcher p. 75)

the squadron divides at 10 p.m. Belcher's record form: 'Left Beechey Island, Saturday, 14th August, at ten P.M. Proceeding towards Sir Robert Inglis Bay, westerly.' He and Kellett agree to try to communicate at 77 N and 105 W (Belcher pp. 82, 85)
passes Cape Grinnell in the morning and Cape Osborn about noon; the icy barrier Penny had reported was not there, and the ships cross Baring Bay (Belcher p. 83). Position is Cape Osborn
stated observed position: landed at Point Hogarth, Lyall Bluff, to examine a natural stone pillar, and observed for latitude, longitude and variation (Belcher pp. 84-85)

secured in Northumberland Sound at the head of Queen's Channel, then moved to a sheltered berth on the opposite side. 'From that spot the ship never moved... that season!' (Belcher pp. 88-89; position from M'Dougall p. 246)
stated position: a boat-and-sledge party takes possession of Exmouth Island on the anniversary of Algiers (Belcher p. 105)

stated observing position at the 'Land's End of North Cornwall'; the west extreme at 77 deg 39 min N, 96 deg 15 min W, and an island glimpsed from the hill probably in 77 deg 45 min N (Belcher p. 114)
stated position: Pell Point, the northernmost fixed position of the autumn journey, then a seventeen-mile open-water pull to Table Island (Belcher pp. 116-117)
Belcher regains his cabin about 4.30; winter completely established, the ships frozen in and the observatory built (Belcher pp. 121-122)
Assistance and Pioneer cut out of Northumberland Sound and leave their first winter quarters after eleven months (Belcher p. 344; M'Dougall p. 383)

a spring-tide gale drives the ships west towards Cape Majendie; they escape into a new anchorage Belcher names Port Refuge. It is the same gale that killed Bellot in Wellington Channel and blew the Resolute out of Dealy Island (Belcher pp. 356-357). Position inferred

blasted and cut out of Port Refuge after thirteen days. Belcher's reason for not making for Beechey Island: it was 'one hundred and twenty miles as the crow flies... too far to transport crew, invalids, and effects, if compelled to abandon next season' (Belcher pp. 361-363)
stated position: blocked again about ten miles north-east of Cape Osborn, off Cape Eden; the Pioneer separated. Belcher's volume I stops eleven days later (Belcher pp. 366, 383)

stated winter position: Assistance and Pioneer in Disaster Bay, about fifty-two miles nearly north of the North Star at Beechey Island (M'Dougall p. 406). The date is the settling of the winter, not an observation
Assistance and Pioneer abandoned at 5 a.m. at the floe edge two miles south of Cape Osborn; the crews take to the boats (M'Dougall pp. 435, 437)

all boats alongside the North Star at Beechey Island by 5 p.m.; an hour and a half after Belcher arrives, the Phoenix and Talbot appear off Cape Riley with news of the war with Russia (M'Dougall pp. 437-438)
de Bray sets the marble tablet to Bellot on the Beechey monument and three volleys are fired; at 1 p.m. the three ships slip from the ice, the North Star in tow of the Phoenix (M'Dougall pp. 439-440)
home in the first week of October 1854. The court martial sat aboard HMS Waterloo at Sheerness on 18-20 October (M'Dougall pp. 447-451)
the Prince Albert declared ready for sea and towed out of Aberdeen by the steam-tug Victory at 8.10 p.m. (Snow pp. 21-29)
anchored at Long Hope, Orkney, in a westerly gale; the hold restowed. She weighed on the 9th, cleared the Orkneys on the 10th, and never cast anchor again until Aberdeen (Snow pp. 33-35, 381)
stated position: 'a good run of 140 miles, the best we had yet experienced' (Snow p. 37)
the heaviest gale of the passage; at noon they made themselves ninety-five miles from Cape Farewell but could not raise the land. Position computed from that distance (Snow pp. 52-53)
stated position: sounded in 78 fathoms, speckled sand, stone and rock; variation by azimuth 62 deg 15 min W (Snow p. 60)
driven past Disko in heavy weather, lying in an open bay on the west coast, where the boat's crew found a European's solitary grave (Snow pp. 65-73). Position inferred
off the Woman Islands and Upernavik at 5 a.m.; Snow's long boat journey ashore with the mails in rain and mist (Snow pp. 82-85)
completely beset at six o'clock, the Devil's Thumb bearing south-east about thirty miles; warps, ice-anchors and windlass all failed. Position computed from that bearing and distance (Snow p. 106)
stated position, Sabine Islands bearing north-east about ten miles; the mizen-topmast struck, boats out on the ice and provisions on deck against a nip (Snow pp. 140-141)

stated position: twelve miles made good on the direct course through the whole passage of Melville Bay, while the government ships and Penny had made only thirty miles in five weeks (Snow pp. 151-153)
'at ten A.M. we passed Captain Austin's fleet, still beset' (Snow p. 166). Position inferred
Cape York: Snow meets Caloosa (afterwards Erasmus York), the messenger Cheepchow bearing Penny's note of the day before, and the boy Aladoonga (Snow pp. 189-197)
casts off the Resolute's tow-rope at 2 p.m. about fifty-two miles from Cape Hay; Austin calls after them 'Success to you, my fine fellows!' Position computed from that distance (Snow pp. 234-235)
the fog lifts on the Byam Martin mountains and Lancaster Sound is found free of ice (Snow pp. 237-240)

Snow lands with great difficulty at Whaler Point, Port Leopold: James Clark Ross's house, steam launch and depot are all there and the cylinders on the flagstaff hold nothing about Franklin - 'they had not been there' (Snow pp. 247-254)
off Fury Beach and stopped by heavy hummocky ice on every side. Snow begged for a boat to land and was refused; at 4 p.m. all hands were told the vessel was returning to England (Snow pp. 255-260)
falls in with the American brig Advance at the entrance of Prince Regent Inlet; Snow visits her and meets De Haven and Kane. Position inferred (Snow pp. 289-303)

lands at Cape Riley, copies out Ommanney's notice of the 23rd and De Haven's of that morning, and finds bleached canvas, rope with the Chatham Dock-yard navy mark, a bored bone and four or five circles of stones (Snow pp. 306-320)
boat away at 3 a.m. and landed at Possession Bay through heavy surf; a cairn found on a rise with a line of stones from it (Snow pp. 340-343)

Pond's Bay: a night boat expedition examines four prominent points, rockets and blue lights are burnt, an Inuit encampment is found and no other trace; a cairn built on a peak with a notice in it (Snow pp. 349-361)
stated position, running down Davis Strait before a strong northerly breeze at seven or eight knots with scarcely any ice (Snow pp. 363-365)
towed over the Aberdeen bar after dark. 'As it was quite dark, few witnessed our arrival, and I was not sorry for it.' (Snow pp. 380-381)

sails from Beechey Island carrying Belcher's despatches home (Kennedy p. 169)
off Cape Farewell homeward; St Kilda twelve days later (Kennedy p. 170). Position inferred
anchors in Aberdeen harbour in the afternoon, six weeks from Beechey Island and sixteen months from England (Kennedy p. 170)
the Fox sails from Aberdeen - a 177-ton steam yacht bought by Lady Franklin, with a crew of twenty-five, seventeen of whom had been in the Arctic before (McClintock p. 21)

beset in the middle ice of Melville Bay, later than any voyage to Barrow Strait except Parry's in 1824 and the Prince Albert's in 1851. The date is calculated back from 242 days in the pack; the position is approximate (McClintock pp. 41-42, 109)

escapes the pack in a heavy swell in the early hours of Sunday the 25th, having been carried 1194 geographical (1385 statute) miles in 242 days - 'the longest drift I know of.' The position is approximate (McClintock pp. 105-109)
anchored at Holsteinborg (Sisimiut) and moored to the rocks; the ship refitted and the whole attempt begun again from the beginning (McClintock p. 111)

The day within August is approximate
'we were then about half-way through Bellot Strait!' The tides in the strait run at six or seven knots and the ship was driven back repeatedly; four attempts were needed (McClintock pp. 181-182)

winter quarters at the eastern end of Bellot Strait, in an anchorage McClintock named Port Kennedy 'after my predecessor, the discoverer of Bellot Strait, of which it is decidedly the port.' The date within September is approximate (McClintock p. 199)
the Fox gets out of Port Kennedy in the second week of August after eleven months, having sent out three sledge divisions in the spring. The exact day is not fixed here
passes Fury Beach going north up Prince Regent Inlet, homeward (McClintock p. 335). The day is approximate
arrives in the English Channel, nineteen days from Greenland; McClintock lands at Portsmouth and reaches London on the evening of the 21st to tell the Admiralty what he had found (McClintock p. 348)
the Gabriel, the Michael and a pinnace leave Ratcliffe on the Thames
the Queen waves from a window at Greenwich as they pass
Shetland, after being held back by wind

first sight of new land, named Queen Elizabeth's Foreland; probably Resolution Island
Christopher Hall lands and names Hall's Island; the ship enters the water Frobisher takes for a strait

first meeting and trading with Inuit; five men take a hired Inuit pilot ashore, row out of sight and are never seen again. Position inferred from the English statement in 1577 that the men were lost about fifty leagues farther in than York Sound
Frobisher lures a kayaker alongside with a hand-bell and lifts him bodily aboard, man and kayak, to hold against the five; date approximate
turns for England with thirteen men and boys left fit
off the Orkneys

London; the captive and his kayak are a wonder to the whole city, and a lump of black stone comes ashore with them

waypoints.note: the Ayde, the Gabriel and the Michael leave Harwich with about 120 men
north about Scotland, by the Orkneys

the fleet works back east and north through the ice towards the mines; ships are scattered and about twenty boats and pinnaces lost in the storms
the order is given to disembark all men and stores on the Countess of Warwick's Island, now Kodlunarn

the fleet reaches England, some in one place and some in another

tracking along the ice-belt under the Greenland shore
aground under the ice-foot near Cape Thomas Leiper
warped into Rensselaer Harbour; she never came out

karluk-cae-001.title: The Karluk: Esquimalt to Wrangel Island, 1913-1914

waypoints.note: the Karluk leaves Esquimalt, British Columbia, under Robert Bartlett
Nome, Alaska
leaves Port Clarence at 3 a.m. for the Arctic
Point Hope: Panyurak and Asatshak join the ship
jammed in the ice off the Seahorse Islands, twenty-five miles southwest of Point Barrow
off Cape Smythe: Kataktovik, John Hadley and Kuraluk with Kiruk, Helen and Mugpi come aboard
beset in the ice near Camden Bay, the ship's farthest east, about 225 miles from Point Barrow; she never moves under her own power again
Stefansson leaves with McConnell, Wilkins, Jenness, Panyurak and Asatshak to hunt caribou ashore; a gale takes the ship west and they never rejoin her
drifting west past Point Barrow; position inferred from the narrative
the farthest north of the drift, latitude 73 degrees; the longitude is inferred
drifting southwest toward Herald Island; position inferred
the last observation taken aboard: 72 degrees 11 minutes north, 174 degrees 36 minutes west
the ice opens the ship's side; Bartlett gives the order, all hands abandon ship
the Karluk sinks at 4 p.m. in thirty-eight fathoms, about sixty miles north of Herald Island; Shipwreck Camp is built on the floe
Anderson, Barker, King and Brady leave Shipwreck Camp for Herald Island and are never seen again
Mackay, Murray, Beuchat and Morris leave the camp on their own, man-hauling; they are never seen again
Bartlett leaves Shipwreck Camp with the main body for Wrangel Island
the party lands at Icy Spit on the north coast of Wrangel Island
the King and Winge takes off the Rodgers Harbour camp; the Bear lands all the survivors at Nome on 13 September
leaves Bache Peninsula with Nukapinguaq and Inuetuk, two teams of twelve dogs
head of Flagler Fiord: the land almost bare of snow, days of slow travel over rock and gravel
several routes onto the Flagler Glacier and the pass reconnoitred and abandoned; the crossing to Axel Heiberg Island given up
back through Rice Strait, heading south down the east coast of Ellesmere Island instead
Clarence Head: better going from here south
Craig Harbour: nobody had been there since Corporal McLean's visit a year before. No sign of Krüger
starting back north; Stallworthy falls 9 m into a crevasse near Boger Point and is hauled out on a harpoon line by Nukapinguaq and Inuetuk
back at Bache Peninsula. No trace of the Krüger expedition found

kruger-1930-003.title: Stallworthy's search around Axel Heiberg Island, 1932

waypoints.note: the whole convoy leaves Bache Peninsula: eight teams, 124 dogs, 60 days' rations for seven men
head of Flagler Fiord, then west up the valley on river ice and over the divide to the depot laid the previous October

an advancing glacier now blocks the old route through the pass: loads packed 800 m up a rocky hillside, sledges hauled up empty by relays of 25 to 30 dogs, then a 1.2 km descent lined down singly on harpoon lines, twelve hours' work
Bay Fiord: the party splits. Stallworthy takes the north shore with Eetookashoo, Qaavigarsuaq and Kahdi, three sledges and 49 dogs
May Point, Eureka Sound: herds of eleven and then nineteen muskoxen, all spared
camp at Depot Point, where Krüger's support sledges had turned back two years before
the next three points west checked as far as the mouth of Mokka Fiord; a small cairn at Blaamenden crossed to and found old and empty
south of Skraeling Point: canned dog food down to three feeds, hunting parties returning empty-handed, and Stallworthy at last allows six muskoxen to be shot
across the isthmus of Schei Peninsula, which Sverdrup had thought an island; a small cairn examined, probably an old Inuit one
forced right over to the mouth of Otto Fiord to avoid rough ice in Nansen Sound - the same ice that had probably pushed Krüger onto the Ellesmere shore in 1930
the northern tip of Axel Heiberg Island, now Cape Stallworthy: a mile of beach searched, a lookout climbed, a water sky less than 80 km north
Cape Thomas Hubbard: Peary's cairn spotted only on looking back from further west. Krüger's note of 24 April 1930 taken out of it - the only trace any search ever found
south across the mouth of Rens Fjord, 65 km in a day on good ice

Cape Northwest: heavy pressure ice drives the sledges onto the ice-foot and inland. Meighen Island in sight across Sverdrup Channel, judged 100 to 115 km off (it is 45), with rough ice all the way. The crossing is abandoned
25 km short of Cape Southwest after an almost continuous 43-hour march; the last bacon, the last dog pemmican and all the spare sealskins fed to the dogs, and six dogs killed to feed the rest
Cape Southwest: Hamilton's note and the depot. Four days' rest and feeding
MacMillan's 1916 cairn found with messages from MacMillan and from Joy in 1927 and nothing from Krüger; Stallworthy concludes the missing party never came this way
towards Cape Sherwood: seven caribou killed after a careful stalk, all thin and three of them young
round Hyperite Point; camp on the east side of Ulvingen Island. Five more dogs killed next morning
Kahdi shoots a 140 kg seal with blubber more than 6 cm thick, and the crisis passes; a bear and further seals follow
leaves Ulvingen Island north up Eureka Sound and east into Bay Fiord
head of Bay Fiord: almost no snow, sledging through mud and 25 cm of water, then a 3 km rock canyon with frozen waterfalls where the sledges were dismantled to pass
Bache Peninsula, stopped by a polynya 1.6 km short and the last lap walked. 65 days, not less than 2250 km, twelve dogs and nine muskoxen
parts from Stallworthy near the head of Bay Fiord about noon and takes the south shore, with Nukapinguaq and Kahkachoo and the support teams of Inuetuk and Seekeeunguaq
Stor Island
Raanes Peninsula: a depot of pemmican cached for the support drivers' return
Ulvingen Island; a small bear killed and fed to the dogs
Hyperite Point: signs of caribou and muskoxen, one small caribou killed, no sign of Krüger on the coast
Cape Southwest: the cape and its old cairns searched, nothing found; two small bears killed; the support depot cached and Inuetuk and Seekeeunguaq left to put up meat
south-west towards Cornwall Island through rough ice, deep snow and fog; the last pemmican fed to the dogs
Cornwall Island: one sledge, most of the provisions and the weakest dogs left behind; eight hours with Nukapinguaq breaking trail to the northern tip

northern point of Cornwall Island: Joy's cairns found, no sign of Krüger. Hamilton turns back on Nukapinguaq's advice that bears do not use the multiyear pack and that there is no game on the Ringnes islands
back at Cape Southwest; four of the dogs left on Cornwall Island had died and five more died on the crossing. Bear meat cached by the support party saves the rest
Glacier Fiord: three muskoxen shot out of a herd of eighteen
Goose Point, the north-west tip of Bjorne Peninsula: coastline and headland searched, nothing
Baumann Fiord in deep snow; five more dogs dead of starvation, and four muskoxen shot on Bjorne Peninsula
Hoved Island, after a two-day blizzard that nearly broke the snow house. A charging bear gashes Nukapinguaq's hip before he kills it

the overland crossing from the head of Stenkul Fiord to Makinson Inlet, three days. Nukapinguaq had shown Krüger this route on the map at Bache Peninsula; an old RCMP cairn on it holds no message from him
head of Makinson Inlet; two days' rest, sledges and harness repaired
across Talbot Inlet through very rough ice with open water offshore; stopped at Cape Dunsterville by water lapping the cliffs and forced over a glacier
Cape Isabella: open water again drives them over another glacier, lined down a precipitous descent. Three dogs die
the cache at Fram Havn: food for the men and old bacon for the dogs
Bache Peninsula. 49 days, about 1510 km, 17 dogs lost, seven muskoxen shot
leaves Dundas Harbour with Kellekte and Keepoomee, two sledges and 31 dogs; Keepoomee's sledge breaks through thin ice hidden by new snow at the west headland
across the mouth of Croker Bay, west towards Cuming Inlet, with long detours round polynyas and wide leads and a trail chopped through pressure ice
about 200 km west of the post: steep hard-packed drifts running from the cliffs into brash ice and open water, ruts cut for the runners to stop the sledges sliding sideways
a 400 m snow slope with impassable brash below; Dersch cuts steps to the top and sees three worse ahead. The sledges are unloaded and tipped end over end to turn them
an inlet followed 15 km to its head looking for a break in the cliffs; none found, and the ice will not freeze
back at Dundas Harbour

mcclure-investigator-023.title: HMS Investigator, Plymouth to the Bay of Mercy, 1850-1853

waypoints.note: sails from Plymouth with the Enterprise, bound for Bering Strait by Cape Horn
leaves Honolulu, provisioned for the Arctic
McClure writes his despatch to the Admiralty setting out what he will do if he loses the Enterprise
first ice, on the 166th meridian; walrus in herds along the pack edge
rounds Point Barrow at midnight in thick weather and enters the Arctic Ocean
Jones' Island, lat. 70 deg 33 min N, long. 150 deg 16 min W; visited by twenty-four people in two umiaks
lands near Point Warren; a drawn bow, then trade, through Miertsching (position inferred)
Cape Bathurst (position inferred from the place)
off Cape Parry; new land seen to the north-east (position inferred)
lands and names Baring Island and Nelson Head (position inferred)
most advanced position of the season, lat. 73 deg 10 min N, long. 117 deg 10 min W, thirty miles short of Barrow Strait
beset for the winter at lat. 73 deg 50 min N, long. 117 deg 55 min W, beside the Princess Royal Islands
free after nearly ten months in one spot
turned back twenty-five miles from Barrow Strait at lat. 73 deg 43 min 43 sec N, long. 115 deg 32 min 30 sec W
rounds Nelson Head southward to try the west side of Banks Land
noon position off the Norway and Robilliard Islands, west coast of Banks Land (the printed longitude is garbled in the scan and read here as 123 deg 52 min 30 sec W)
Ballast Beach, lat. 74 deg 25 min N, long. 122 deg W
aground in the night, then afloat in the bay McClure names the Bay of Mercy
abandoned where she lay, twenty months after entering the bay
clears Plymouth with the Investigator
a fine breeze carries the Enterprise through Bering Strait, a fortnight behind McClure
anchors at Port Clarence and meets Captain Moore of HMS Plover
leaves Sitka for Hong Kong, the season lost
back north past the Diomede Islands
near Point Barrow: Inupiat come out over the ice, give the local place names and draw a chart of the coast
off the mouth of Prince of Wales Strait; the Princess Royal Islands seen to the east
lands on the Princess Royal Islands and finds McClure's notice in a copper cylinder: the Investigator had wintered four miles north-east of them
furthest north of the season, blocked by ice and unable even to see Melville Island
into winter quarters at Walker Bay on the west coast of Victoria Island
leaves Walker Bay after nearly eleven months
driven back into Prince of Wales Strait by ice off Bear Island
working south and east through Dolphin and Union Strait
Coronation Gulf
settles for the winter at Cambridge Bay (Iqaluktuuttiaq); Copper Inuit visit the same day
a sledge party finds Dr John Rae's record of 13 August 1851 on the Victoria Island shore
furthest north of the spring journey, a cairn on an island in Victoria Strait; the party turns back short of King William Island
the Finlayson Islands: a piece of worked fir with a copper door-hasp bearing the Queen's mark, picked up at high-water mark (date reconstructed from the narrative)
frozen in for a third winter at Camden Bay on the Alaskan coast
meets HMS Plover off Point Barrow: the first mail in three years and one month
gets a sight of Old England, five years and four months out
Alert and Discovery leave Portsmouth at 4 p.m.
Godhavn (Qeqertarsuaq), Disco; date approximate
Proven (Kangersuatsiaq): three days engaging Inuit dog drivers, among them Hans Hendrik
Upernavik; date approximate
Cape York after the Melville Bay crossing; date approximate
Cape Sabine rounded, entering Kane Basin
Dobbin Bay and Cape Hawks, after ten days' battle with heavy ice
Discovery goes into winter quarters in Discovery Harbour
Alert reaches Floeberg Beach, 82 deg 27 min N: the highest latitude a ship had wintered
Alert breaks out of the ice
the two ships rejoin off Discovery Harbour; date approximate
Alert enters Valentia Harbour, Ireland
both ships enter Portsmouth Harbour

nares-greely-024.title: The Proteus voyage to Lady Franklin Bay, July-August 1881

waypoints.note: the Proteus passes the narrows of St. John's, Newfoundland, at noon
Godhavn (Qeqertarsuaq), where Dr. Pavy joined; date approximate
Upernavik
Proven (Kangersuatsiaq): Lockwood brings back Jens Edward and Thorlip Frederik Christiansen in the launch Lady Greely
Cape York after Melville Bay; date approximate
Cape Sabine; date approximate
the Proteus anchors to the floe in Discovery Harbour; Fort Conger is built on the shore

norse-helluland-009.title: Leif Eiriksson's voyage as the sagas tell it, about 1000

waypoints.note: Brattahlid in Eiriksfjord: Leif buys Bjarni's ship and sails with thirty-five men (saga)
out of the Eastern Settlement fjords into the Davis Strait
HELLULAND: no grass, great glaciers behind, the land between sea and glacier like one flat rock. Landfall placed on the east coast of Qikiqtaaluk; the saga gives no coordinates
MARKLAND: low-lying, wooded, wide white sands. Usually read as the Labrador coast

VINLAND: an island north of the mainland, then a sound, a river out of a lake, houses built for the winter. L'Anse aux Meadows is the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland; the saga does not name it

norse-helluland-010.title: Thorfinn Karlsefni's voyage as Eiriks saga rauda tells it, about 1005

waypoints.note: Brattahlid: the expedition is agreed, 160 people in several ships (saga)
the Western Settlement (Vestribygd), the last Norse habitation
Bjarneyjar, the Bear Isles: departure point, position unknown, placed here in the Disko Bay region on Nansen's reading
HELLULAND after two doegr at sea with northerly winds: flat stones two men long, arctic foxes in abundance
MARKLAND after two more doegr, course changed from south to south-east; Bjarney (Bear Island) offshore to the south-east
Kjalarnes (Keelness) and Furdustrandir, the Wonder Beaches: long sands, a ship's keel found. Position wholly conjectural
Straumsfjord, first winter; then Hop further south. Neither has been located

norse-helluland-011.title: The clerics' voyage north into Baffin Bay, about 1267

waypoints.note: Kroksfjardarheidr, the Nordrsetur hunting station: Nansen identifies Kroksfjord with the Vaigat, about 70.5 N. The priests' ship sails north from here
north along the coast until the land sank below the horizon; then a southerly gale and thick weather drove them off

FURTHEST NORTH, about 74 N near Melville Bay on Nansen's reckoning from the sailing times. Many islands, seals, whales, a great number of bears; ancient Skraeling dwelling places they could not land at
three doegr back south; Skraeling dwellings found on islands south of Snaefell
back at Kroksfjardarheidr on St James's day after one long day's rowing
home to Gardar in the Eastern Settlement

norse-helluland-012.title: The Nordrsetur: the Greenlanders' northern hunting grounds

waypoints.note: the Western Settlement, the northern limit of Norse habitation and the start of the summer hunt
Greipar, a named Nordrsetur station; Storm put it about 67 N
Disko Bay, the driftwood coast; Nansen argues the hunt centred here and to the south
Kroksfjardarheidr: booths and houses, the furthest regularly used station
Kingittorsuaq Island, about 73 N: three cairns and a runestone, the northernmost Norse trace known

oxford-ellesmere-1934-001.title: The Signalhorn, London to Etah, July-August 1934

waypoints.note: leaves St Katherine's Dock, London, in the chartered 100-ton sealer Signalhorn
off Holsteinsborg (Sisimiut) in thick mist; first land seen since Scotland, a rock awash they only just avoided
Godhavn (Qeqertarsuaq): the sectional winter hut is found waiting; Stallworthy barters for dog lines, whips and harness and picks the dogs
Jakobshavn (Ilulissat): dogs and dried fish taken aboard
leaves Godhavn with the hut, seventy-one dogs and all the dog food the captain would allow
Thule (Uummannaq) reached and left the same day
Robertson Bay: telegraphic permission to engage Nukapinguaq and Enilungwa, Inuatuk and Natuk; equipment traded at Siorapaluk and a cache made
leaves Robertson Bay for the Ellesmere coast; seven walrus killed among the floes; Ellesmere Island sighted that evening
pack ice blocks the whole of Smith Sound; landing near Cape Hatherton, cache of food and ammunition left
the captain makes for Etah and waits
second attempt at Smith Sound: the pack is still unbroken and now reaches south of the Cape Hatherton cache; the captain abandons the attempt
the Signalhorn leaves her moorings off Etah and steams out of Foulke Fjord, morsing a farewell on the siren

oxford-ellesmere-1934-002.title: Moore, Stallworthy, Nukapinguaq and Inuatuk to Grant Land, April-May 1935

waypoints.note: Moore, Stallworthy, Nukapinguaq and Inuatuk drive north from the summit of the ravine behind Etah at noon, in a gale, with two Inughuit sledges in support
the main pemmican depot at Cache Point after twelve hours' travel; -32 F and a biting north wind; Humphreys's party found asleep here
north along the Greenland shore ice, average load about 700 lb a sledge
Peabody Bay, across the front of the Humboldt Glacier: four seals taken at breathing holes; two Inughuit hunters met, out of food and killing their dogs to feed the rest
a polar bear run down at an iceberg after a chase of several hours; fifty-nine hungry dogs get their first proper feed
Cape Calhoun at the entrance to Kennedy Channel: the two supporting Inughuit sledges turn back for Greenland
held two days in camp on the Greenland side of Kennedy Channel by wind and drift; sledges repaired
Kennedy Channel crossed in poor visibility and snow; Nukapinguaq leads the party straight over though he can see only a few yards
Fort Conger reached with exhausted dogs after a long detour round rough ice at the entrance to Lady Franklin Bay

two days' rest at Fort Conger: Peary's hut occupied and the Union Jack flown over it, a record left in a cairn on the hills behind, Amundsen's 1917 cache examined and the Nares expedition's coal seam of 1875 used for cooking

the east end of Lake Hazen after three days: the ice four to five feet thick, and within minutes holes bored and Arctic char six inches to a foot long coming up; the fish prove far smaller than Peary's account promised

the plan is cut down: Moore and Nukapinguaq go on alone with one sledge and the best dogs while Stallworthy and Inuatuk stay at the lake to fish; they cross to the north side and climb a winding valley behind the Garfield Range in thigh-deep snow
the Gilman Glacier climbed at its extreme western edge, steps cut and the kit carried up; camp at 3000 feet on the ice-cap

a prominent 9000-foot summit in the United States Range climbed, the last 300 feet along a razor-edged ridge; from it a great range is seen stretching north and named the British Empire Range, and Nukapinguaq points out the sea ice of Clements Markham Inlet

the farthest point, about latitude 82 degrees 25 minutes north. With pemmican for one more day out and the dogs failing, Moore takes Nukapinguaq's advice and turns back. Longitude here is inferred from the route; the paper gives only the latitude
back down the glacier at a gallop; three caribou shot by Nukapinguaq, the first meat killed since Peabody Bay
Lake Hazen again: Stallworthy and Inuatuk have fished almost without stopping and have taken only enough for a daily feed, and three Arctic hares
Fort Conger after two days, the dogs completely exhausted; one sledge abandoned and the party reduced to two teams
Kennedy Channel recrossed quickly, keeping to mid-channel; the small depots laid on the way north are used, oil runs out and seal blubber and sledge boards are burnt for cooking
Cape Calhoun: open water and seal at last. Inuatuk crosses thin ice to save a large seal, and about 600 lb of meat is hauled up on to the shore ice
Cache Point rounded on the shore ice with difficulty; Smith Sound now open water to the south on the Greenland side, and fresh sledge tracks show the other parties have gone home
Etah, in the worst snowstorm of the journey, after a journey of about 900 miles

oxford-ellesmere-1934-003.title: Humphreys and Haig-Thomas through Grinnell Land and Ellesmere Land, April-May 1935

waypoints.note: Humphreys and Haig-Thomas, with Utah, Kokachingwa, Kuchiketo and Kokochea, are the first party away from Etah; the dogs bolt on a steep slope near the divide and the sledge stops a foot from the edge
Hatherton Bay cache; the only snow iglu built on the trip, the Inughuit preferring the pyramid tents
the main cache at Cache Point at 8.30; eighty-four and a half tins of dog pemmican of 48 lb each are counted and split three ways with the Grant Land party
north on the sea ice then west towards Pim Island; two seals shot at breathing holes; camp on the sea ice
Fram Haven: stores drawn from the abandoned police depot, a list left and the boxes replaced
Cape Camperdown: bad ice, pressure ridges and deep snow, no seal holes and many old bear tracks
the abandoned police post at Bache Peninsula; Haig-Thomas shoots five of six seals in open water in Flagler Fjord; Humphreys goes inland with Bentham, who is geologizing
north again along the ice-foot to the Cape Camperdown cache; reindeer clothes and second sleeping bags left behind in the mild weather
Victoria Head, by way of Cape Albert and Bartlett Bay, past the remains of a landslide whose boulders lie fifty yards out on the sea ice

Franklin Pierce Bay, just north of Norman Lockyer Island. Driving up the valley at the head of the bay for the glacier the chart shows, they find no glacier at all, and recent musk ox tracks and dung where musk ox were thought exterminated
round Cape Harrison to Copes Bay, opposite Cape Field
the Parrish Glacier at the head of the fjord: glare ice, the glacier itself almost bare of snow
Utah and Kokachingwa turn back; the rest drive straight up the glacier on a near-perfect surface, leaving pemmican near the top for the dogs' sake

the farthest point on the Grinnell Land ice-cap. From the camp a single high conical peak is seen about fifty miles west and a bearing taken. North of the camp the snow turns deep and soft; after two days of five hours' pushing the dogs can drag no further and the party turns back in five hours

the isthmus of Cook Peninsula crossed; the first seal taken lying on the ice; Inughuit tent rings noted on a gravel beach, an island on the chart is missing and an uncharted islet is seen in Woodward Bay
Princess Marie Bay crossed to the north coast of Bache Peninsula; snow stops the photography of Woodward and Sawyer Bays
the isthmus of Bache Peninsula crossed in deep snow, all the dogs harnessed to each sledge in turn; a runner is broken dropping down a cliff and one sledge scrapped
back at Bache station so the Inughuit can dry their clothes and take on seal meat, in which they have more confidence than in pemmican
up Flagler Fjord over glare ice in a wind so strong the sledge is blown sideways; a lemming, the only one of the journey, is caught rolling across the fjord
the isthmus crossed to Bay Fiord past Thumb Mountain, which guards the western portal of the land crossing; a glacier from the south nearly chokes the valley and a detour is made

west along Bay Fiord: herds of musk ox on both shores and herds of caribou, all very tame; a coal seam about two yards wide and fossil wood collected for the geologist; the only Arctic wolf of the expedition follows the hunters into camp
camp on the ice-foot opposite the Gretha Islands; a polar bear tracked and killed, and the Inughuit get the bearskin they came north for

the crossing of Ellesmere Land: sixteen and a half hours by valley and divide from the Bay Fiord coast to a fjord running down to the sea. Humphreys took it for Vendom Fiord; Haig-Thomas and Nukapinguaq held that it was Trold Fiord, and the question is left open in the printed paper
back to Bay Fiord, collecting fossil-bearing rocks near the divide and the rest of the caribou meat
camp at the head of Flagler Fjord; the crossing to Canon Fjord and even the ascent of Mount Moore are given up, the Inughuit wanting to be home before the ice breaks
Bache station, where the geological party is found

Haa Island: about fifteen house sites examined, and from the moss packed in a standing wall a number of artefacts recovered, since deposited in the Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford. In one grave lay a young girl and a baby; the Inughuit said that by the care of its building her people must have loved her very much

the Greenland coast reached north of Cache Point at 1.30 a.m. after one camp on the ice. The undercut ice-foot breaks away under Haig-Thomas's sledge and the dogs drop hanging by their traces; Kokochea cuts the draw-line and is lowered on a rope to haul them out. Two dogs are crushed dead and four never seen again
Etah, after about 800 miles

oxford-ellesmere-1934-004.title: Shackleton and Bentham to Scoresby Bay, April-May 1935

waypoints.note: Shackleton and Bentham leave Etah on a windy sunny afternoon with five sledges, four driven by Inughuit; Porsman and Ahnowka to go the whole way, the younger men in support
across Refuge Harbour, MacMillan's old winter quarters, in an icy wind; the sledges dragged up twenty feet on to the ice-foot at low tide and the party drives into camp frost-bitten
Cache Point: a day spent polishing the scored steel runners, collecting the Bovril dog pemmican and re-sorting the loads
north-west out on to the sea ice on Humphreys's trail, through 60 to 70 degrees of frost; tea boiled at Humphreys's first floe camp
the police depot at Fram Haven after twelve hours through very rough ice, all of it on a trail the first party had made
Cape Albert about six in the morning; reserves of dog feed and provisions cached. Sakeus is disabled by what turns out to be an iron filing in his eye and is bandaged and carried on Porsman's sledge
the old police post at the mouth of Flagler Fjord about three in the afternoon, after a forced march of over fifty miles; Humphreys anaesthetises the eye and takes the filing out
up Flagler Fjord and over the neck of the peninsula, at that point not a mile and a half wide though the maps make it more; the pass only 700 feet above the sea ice
the Sven Hedin Glacier in Woodward Bay: a badly crevassed terminal moraine, a snout sixty feet high and convex, and talus in front of it - all signs, Shackleton judged, of an advancing glacier
back at Bache after a twenty-four hour day of about seventy miles; Bentham has found valuable Cambrian fossils in the ravine behind the post
the depot at Cape Albert emptied and the party heads out into Kane Basin for Scoresby Bay

eighty miles in three days, then a day of chaos: pressure ridges twenty-five feet high, axes in continuous use, and at last a huge palaeocrystic floe of miniature hills and valleys, half-way to Dobbin Bay
stopped by impassable ice near Hayes Point and forced three miles in to the mainland; camp just south of the point, where Bentham collects Silurian trilobites, gastropods and brachiopods
the Darling Peninsula: a bay with a ten-foot gravel bank and a flat shingly plain, wind-free, which they christen Aerodrome Bay as a landing ground for aeroplanes

south of Cape Fraser the ice-foot disappears under blocks thirty to forty feet up the hillside; half an hour to lower the sledges to the sea ice. Camp three miles south of Scoresby Bay, where in the night a great mass of the ice-foot falls on the floe and shatters it

Scoresby Bay proves to be a long inlet running south, not the bay on the chart. The Victoria and Albert Mountains stand at its head seven or eight miles off, not twenty miles inland as Nares mapped them from the deck of his ship; one peak rises over 5000 feet, ringed by ice at about 2000

Shackleton takes time signals on a two-valve Stratton receiver at Cape Norton Shaw and hears news from Daventry, Pittsburgh, Philadelphia, Schenectady and Cincinnati. It is too cold for useful sun observations and he falls ill

Bentham, without snowshoes, flounders four hours up a foothill of the main peak and turns back with snow-blindness coming on; the climb is abandoned. The whole of Scoresby Bay proves Silurian as far north as Cape M'Clintock
south again with lighter sledges; the last dog feed is finished at Cape Hawks, south of Dobbin Bay. Total bag for the whole journey so far: one Arctic hare
a forced march of fifty miles without sleep to Cape Albert
Bache Peninsula in glorious weather; the Inughuit go straight out and bring in four seal for the ravenous dogs

after five days' collecting by Bentham in Princess Marie Bay and a search by Shackleton for Inughuit remains in Alexandra Fiord, the party leaves for Etah with three sledges, one having been smashed beyond repair
forty miles and fifteen hours out into Smith Sound
a blizzard strikes in mid-Sound; the tent takes five men to raise and holds for thirty-six hours. They find afterwards that they were camped within half a mile of open water

Hatherton Bay in the afternoon after sixteen hours on the trail, having ferried the sledges on floating pans round a point where the ice-foot had collapsed under one of Humphreys's sledges and crushed six of his dogs
Etah in the early hours, after a journey of 800 miles. The Inughuit leave the same day for their sealing grounds in the south

pole-seekers-from-ellesmere-006.title: Peary's 1909 route from Cape Columbia, by his own latitudes

waypoints.note: Peary leaves the Roosevelt at Cape Sheridan
Crane City, Cape Columbia: the whole party assembled
24 men, 19 sledges, 133 dogs leave the land
beyond Markham's British record of 83 deg 20 min; halted at the edge of a lead. Longitude inferred
Dr Goodsell turns back at about 84 deg 29 min. Longitude inferred
Camp 19: Borup turns back; later fixed at 85 deg 23 min. Longitude inferred
Marvin's observation, 85 deg 48 min. Longitude inferred
86 deg 38 min; Marvin turns back from here and dies on the return
Bartlett turns back at 87 deg 47 min, the last man sent home
Peary's reckoning places the party at the Pole; disputed

late evening: off Schomberg Point, having steamed and drifted north through broken but crowded ice
a good lead west to the north end of Byam Martin Island; anchors, builds a small cairn in the new snow and leaves a record cylinder
the first clear day for a week; crosses to Melville Island at Consett Head, a dozen muskoxen grazing on the lowland by the beach

midnight: anchors close inshore in 25 fathoms off Palmer Point. The magnetic compasses have been useless for days, the north point often fixed on the ship's head whatever her course
afternoon: Dealy Island. Examines Kellett's 1853 depot from HMS Resolute, torn open by bears, and Bernier's 1909 record; takes away a few sound tins, including ox-cheek soup made in 1850
Winter Harbour, Melville Island. Parry Rock carries the names of Hecla and Griper, Bernier's 1909 sovereignty plate, and a bottle left by Inspector Joy in 1929; the St. Roch adds her record

whaling-017.title: The Baffin Bay Circuit: the whalers' season, 1817-1860s

waypoints.note: 1. Late March or early April: the outward passage keeps well south of Kap Farvel (Cape Farewell) to stay clear of the East Greenland ice drifting westward round the cape
2. April and May: the Southwest Fishing, off Resolution Island and the southeast Baffin coast - the season's first whales
3. May: the fleet cruises diagonally northeast across Davis Strait to the East Side, the West Greenland coast
4. May and early June: the Disko fishery, Qeqertarsuaq (Godhavn) and the bays around Disko. Some ships sailed here direct and started fishing before the end of April
5. June: north past Upernavik along the lane between the land-fast ice and the Middle Ice - the pack filling the centre of Baffin Bay between about 65 and 75 degrees north
6. Mid-June: the Devil's Thumb (Kullorsuaq), the recognised gate into Melville Bay

7. Late June: Melville Bay (Qimusseriarsuaq). Warping, tracking and sawing docks in the fast ice; a fortnight was a good passage, fifty days a bad one, and this is where the fleet was destroyed in 1830
8. About 1 July: breaking out off Cape York into open water. Vaughan: in only four years between 1817 and 1848 did the whalers fail to reach the North Water
9. Early July: the North Water (Pikialasorsuaq), crossing south of the Carey Islands. Goodsir knew he was near it when the ship began to lift to the swell
10. Early July: the West Side made near Cape Byam Martin on Bylot Island, at the mouth of Lancaster Sound
11. July: the entrance of Lancaster Sound, and for a few ships the run west along the Devon coast and south into Prince Regent Inlet
12. July and August: Pond's Bay, off Mittimatalik (Pond Inlet) - the best of the West Side. The Cumbrian counted 41 sail here on 14 July 1823
13. August and September: south along the Baffin coast, the fiord fishery, Niginganiq (Isabella Bay) and the floe edge
14. September: Cape Searle, a landmark of the homeward run
15. September: full ships leave for home from Cape Dyer
16. September and October: ships not yet full carry on south into Cumberland Sound and Frobisher Bay for a last effort - almost back in the Southwest Fishing, but further north and closer inshore
